title: Final Capstone Project
description: Plan, build and present a working generative AI application of your own.

lessons.title: Choosing your capstone
lessons.description: Four questions, and why the smallest worthwhile version is the project.
lessons.content:
## Learn

The capstone is one project you plan, build and present. It is what Level 3 of the certification is awarded for.

### What it has to be

**Working.** It runs. Someone else can use it.

**Yours.** You chose it, you scoped it, you built it.

**Small enough to finish.** This is the one people get wrong.

**Honest.** You know and can state what it does badly.

### The six briefs

Six follow, each with a different shape. Read all of them before choosing -- the one that sounds least exciting is sometimes the one you will actually finish.

1. **AI Study Assistant** -- extend module 12's project properly
2. **Resume and Interview Assistant** -- CV feedback and interview practice
3. **PDF Question-Answering Bot** -- module 13's RAG over documents
4. **AI Marketing Assistant** -- copy, variants and a brand voice
5. **AI Customer Support Chatbot** -- grounded answers with escalation
6. **AI Research Assistant** -- search, read, summarise with sources

You may propose your own. It must be comparable in scope and must exercise at least two of: prompting, RAG, agents, a real interface.

### Choosing well

Four questions, in this order.

**1. Would you use it yourself?** The single best predictor of finishing. A project you actually want is one you will debug at eleven at night.

**2. Do you have the material?** RAG projects need documents. A support bot needs a knowledge base. If you would have to invent the content, choose differently or budget time for it.

**3. Can you tell whether it works?** You must be able to mark its output. A project in a subject you do not know is one you cannot evaluate, and evaluation is heavily weighted.

**4. Is it small enough?** Almost everyone chooses something too large. Halve it, then halve it again.

### On scope

The most common failure in this module is not technical. It is choosing a project that needs six weeks and having eight hours.

**A small thing that works and is measured beats a large thing that half-works.** By a wide margin, and the rubric reflects that.

Concretely: three features done properly and evaluated scores far higher than eight features that mostly run.

### What is being marked

Roughly:

- It works, and someone else can use it
- The prompts are tested, not guessed
- It handles failure and refuses when it should
- You measured it and have the numbers
- You can say what it does badly
- You can present it clearly

Notice how much of that is not code. Everything from modules 4, 10, 12 and 13 applies, and a project with excellent code and no evaluation scores below a modest one with good evaluation.

## Demonstrate

Before choosing, test your candidate against the four questions.

Take whichever brief appeals most and write, honestly:

1. Would I use this? When, specifically, in the next month?
2. What material do I need, and do I have it? Where is it right now?
3. How will I know an answer is good? Write one criterion.
4. What is the smallest version that is still worth having?

Question 4 is the important one. Write the smallest version down, and treat that as the project. Anything beyond it is a bonus, not a requirement.

## Practice

Write a one-paragraph project statement:

> I am building [X] for [who]. It takes [input] and produces [output]. The smallest version that is worth having does [three things]. I will know it works because [measurable criterion].

If you cannot fill in the last clause, you have not scoped it yet. Go back to question 3.

Keep this paragraph. It is what you check against when you are tempted to add a seventh feature in week two.

## What to remember

- Working, yours, small enough to finish, and honest about its limits
- Choose what you would actually use; it is the best predictor of finishing
- You must be able to tell whether its output is good, or you cannot evaluate it
- A small measured thing beats a large half-working one, by a lot
- Write the smallest worthwhile version down and treat that as the project

lessons.title: Brief: AI study assistant
lessons.description: Extend module 12 properly; the hard part is questions that test understanding.
lessons.content:
## The brief

An application that helps someone learn from material they supply.

This extends module 12's project. If you built that, you are starting from something working -- which makes this the lowest-risk choice and a perfectly respectable one.

### The smallest worthwhile version

Three features:

1. **Generate practice questions** from pasted material, with answers
2. **Check understanding**: the learner explains from memory, the tool says what is wrong
3. **Explain a concept** at a chosen level

All three are prompts you already have from module 12.

### What makes it more than module 12

Pick one or two:

**Spaced repetition.** Store generated questions and reshow them over increasing intervals. This makes it a tool someone returns to rather than uses once.

**Long material.** Use `chunk_text` from module 12 to handle a whole chapter, summarising each chunk and combining.

**Upload files.** PDF or text rather than pasting.

**A study session.** Several rounds of question, answer, feedback, ending with a score and what to revise.

**Track weak areas.** Record which topics the learner gets wrong and weight future questions toward them.

The last one is the most interesting and the most work.

### What to evaluate

**Question quality.** Take 20 generated questions from material you know. For each: is it answerable from the material, is the given answer correct, does it test understanding or just wording?

**Feedback quality.** Write 10 explanations with deliberate errors -- one wrong fact, one oversimplification, one omission each. Does the tool find them? Report per error type.

**Refusal.** Give it material that does not support the question asked. Does it say so?

### The hard part

**Questions that test understanding rather than recall of wording.** The default output is often "According to the text, what is X?" -- which tests nothing.

Your prompt has to push against this explicitly, and getting it to do so reliably is the real work of this project. It is a prompt engineering problem, not a code problem, and module 4 is where the answer is.

### Watch out for

**Answers that are wrong.** Generated answers are as fallible as anything else. Check them against the material.

**Material too long for one call.** Chunk it, or refuse with a clear message.

**Making it a homework machine.** Module 6's line applies: this should help someone understand, not help them avoid understanding. Consider how the design encourages the right use -- feature 2 does, feature 1 can go either way.

## What good looks like

A study assistant scoring well has **evidence that its questions are good**, not just that it produces questions. Twenty questions marked against the source, with a count of how many tested understanding rather than wording, is what separates this from a demo.

lessons.title: Brief: resume and interview assistant
lessons.description: The no-invention rule, and the number that is the headline result.
lessons.content:
## The brief

A tool that helps someone prepare for a job application: feedback on a CV against a specific role, and interview practice.

### The smallest worthwhile version

Three features:

1. **CV against a job description.** What matches, what is missing, what to emphasise.
2. **Rewrite bullet points** to speak to the role -- using only facts already in the CV.
3. **Interview questions** likely for this role and this CV, with what a good answer covers.

### The rule that defines this project

**Use only facts already in the CV. Never add a skill, tool, achievement or date.**

This is module 4's lesson 11 and it is not optional here. Without it, these tools routinely produce CVs with invented achievements -- which is useless, and genuinely serious to send to an employer.

Build it into the prompt and test specifically that it holds:

> Use only what is stated in the CV. Where the job description asks for something the CV does not evidence, list it under "gaps" rather than inventing coverage.

The **gaps** section turns a temptation to invent into the most useful output the tool produces.

### Extensions

**Mock interview.** Ask a question, the user answers, the tool gives feedback, then asks the next.

**Cover letter draft** from the CV and job description, same no-invention rule.

**Several roles at once.** Which of these five jobs is the best fit, and why.

**Keyword coverage.** Which terms from the job description appear in the CV.

### What to evaluate

**The no-invention rule, hardest.** Take a CV and a job description that ask for something not in the CV. Run it ten times. Count how often something was invented. **This number is the headline result of this project.**

**Gap identification.** Does it correctly find what the CV lacks? Mark against your own reading.

**Rewrite quality.** Are rewritten bullets accurate to the original? Check each against the source line.

**Question relevance.** Would these questions plausibly be asked?

### Watch out for

**Bias.** Module 10's firmest rule: never use AI to evaluate people. This tool helps a **candidate prepare**; it does not screen anyone. Keep that boundary clear in the tool's own description, because a CV tool is one step from a screening tool and the step is a serious one.

**Personal data.** A CV is personal data. If anyone else's CV is involved, module 10's privacy lesson applies in full. For evaluation, use your own or a synthetic one.

**Over-tailoring.** A CV rewritten to match every keyword reads as written by a machine and recruiters notice.

## What good looks like

The headline number is **the invention rate**: how often, across repeated runs against a job description asking for something absent, did it add something that was not in the CV? A project that reports this honestly -- including when it is not zero -- is doing the thing this brief is really about.

lessons.title: Brief: PDF question-answering bot
lessons.description: Module 13 applied; budget most of your time for extraction.
lessons.content:
## The brief

Ask questions of a set of PDF documents and get answers with citations.

This is module 13 applied. If that module's lab went well, this is the natural continuation.

### The smallest worthwhile version

1. **Ingest** one or more PDFs: extract, chunk, embed, store
2. **Answer** questions from the documents
3. **Cite** the source and page for every claim
4. **Refuse** when the documents do not contain the answer

Feature 4 is not optional. A RAG system that cannot refuse is the failure this module warns about.

### What makes this project

**PDF extraction is the real work.** Far more than people expect.

Two columns extract as interleaved nonsense. Headers and footers repeat on every page and pollute every chunk. Tables become word salad. Scanned pages contain no text at all and need OCR.

**Budget most of your time here.** Everything downstream depends on it, and extraction problems are invisible later -- the answers are simply wrong, with no indication why.

### Extensions

**Page-accurate citations.** Not just the document but the page, so a user can check in seconds.

**Multiple documents with filters.** Search only within one document or one date range.

**Comparison.** What do these two documents say differently about X?

**Highlight the passage.** Show the retrieved chunk with the answer's basis marked.

**Handle scanned PDFs** with OCR, and flag when confidence is low.

### What to evaluate

Exactly module 13's assignment:

- **Extraction quality.** Read a page of your extracted text. How much is garbled? Report a percentage.
- **Retrieval accuracy.** Was the right chunk in the top k? Over at least 15 questions.
- **Answer accuracy.** Correct, against your own reading.
- **Citation accuracy.** Does the cited page actually contain the basis for the claim? Check every one.
- **Refusal rate.** Over at least 6 questions the documents cannot answer.

Citation accuracy is the one people assume and do not check. A citation pointing at the wrong page is worse than no citation, because it looks verified.

### Watch out for

**Confidential documents.** Module 10 applies. If the PDFs cannot leave your machine, run the embedding model locally -- `sentence-transformers` does by default -- and consider whether the generation step can happen at all.

**Scanned documents.** A PDF with no extractable text produces empty chunks and a system that silently answers nothing correctly. Detect and report this rather than failing quietly.

**Very large documents.** Chunking a thousand-page PDF takes time and produces a lot of vectors. Start with twenty pages.

## What good looks like

A strong PDF project reports **extraction quality honestly** and **checks every citation**. The projects that score poorly are the ones where extraction was never inspected -- and it shows in the answers without the author knowing why.

lessons.title: Brief: AI marketing assistant
lessons.description: Consistency across formats, and someone else judging whether you achieved it.
lessons.content:
## The brief

A tool that produces marketing copy in a consistent brand voice.

### The smallest worthwhile version

1. **Define a brand voice** once -- tone, vocabulary, what to avoid, examples
2. **Generate copy** for several formats using that voice
3. **Produce variants** for testing -- several versions with different angles

At least three formats. For example: a product description, a social post, an email subject line.

### What makes this project

**Consistency across formats.** The same voice in a 30-word app store description and a 200-word email is harder than it sounds, and it is the actual problem this tool solves.

The technique is a voice definition in the system prompt plus few-shot examples, from module 4 lesson 3. Showing three examples of your voice works far better than describing it.

### Extensions

**Learn the voice from examples.** Paste five pieces of existing copy and have the tool extract the voice rules, then use them.

**A/B variants with a stated hypothesis.** Not just three versions but three versions each testing a different angle, with the angle stated.

**Compliance check.** Does this copy make a claim the product does not support?

**Adapt for a channel.** The same message for a formal newsletter and a casual social post.

**Multilingual**, with a note that a native speaker must check.

### What to evaluate

**Voice consistency.** Generate 15 pieces across your three formats. Have someone else -- not you -- sort them into "sounds like the same brand" and "does not". Report the proportion.

That external judgement matters. You know what you intended, which makes you a poor judge of whether it came through.

**Claim accuracy.** Give it a product description. Count how often generated copy claims something the description does not support. **This is the important number.**

**Variant genuineness.** Are three variants actually different angles, or three rewordings? Mark them.

### Watch out for

**Invented claims.** The headline risk. Marketing copy asserting something untrue is a legal problem as well as a dishonest one. The rule from module 4: *"Do not claim anything the product description does not support. List anything you think is missing separately."*

**Generic output.** The default voice of every model is the same mid-Atlantic corporate register. If your brand voice is that, you have not defined one.

**Advertising rules.** Claims in advertising are regulated in most places. Generated copy is your responsibility.

**Bias in imagery**, if you add image generation. Module 10 lesson 2.

## What good looks like

The strongest submissions have **someone else judging voice consistency** and a **counted claim-accuracy rate**. Self-assessed voice consistency is the most common weakness in this brief, because the author cannot hear the gap between what they meant and what came out.

lessons.title: Brief: AI customer support chatbot
lessons.description: Knowing when not to answer, and reporting both escalation numbers.
lessons.content:
## The brief

A support assistant that answers customer questions from a knowledge base, and escalates when it should not answer.

### The smallest worthwhile version

1. **A knowledge base** -- documentation, FAQs, policies, chunked and retrievable
2. **Answer questions** from it, with sources
3. **Escalate** when the answer is not there, or when the question should not be automated

Feature 3 is the one that makes this a support tool rather than a chatbot.

### What makes this project

**Knowing when not to answer.** A support bot that confidently answers a billing dispute from a shipping policy is worse than one that says "let me get a person".

Three escalation triggers, and you need all three:

**No relevant sources found.** The relevance floor from module 13.

**The question is outside scope.** Complaints, refunds above a threshold, anything legal, anything about an individual account. Define these and detect them.

**The user is frustrated or has asked twice.** A person should take over.

That third one is the difference between a support tool people tolerate and one they resent.

### Extensions

**Conversation memory** within a session, so a follow-up works.

**Confidence indication.** Show the user how well-supported the answer is.

**A summary for the human** when escalating: what was asked, what was tried, what is needed.

**Gap logging.** Record questions that could not be answered -- this becomes the list of documentation to write, and is genuinely the most valuable output of a real support bot.

**Tone control** for a frustrated customer.

### What to evaluate

**Answer accuracy** on 15 questions the knowledge base covers.

**Escalation rate** on 10 questions it should not answer: 5 not in the knowledge base, 5 out of scope.

**False escalation** on questions it should have answered. Escalating everything is safe and useless; report both directions.

**Citation accuracy.**

The two escalation numbers together are the headline. A tool that never escalates and one that always escalates are both failures, and only reporting both shows where yours sits.

### Watch out for

**Confident wrong answers on money.** The highest-cost failure in support. Anything about charges, refunds or account balances should escalate by default.

**Prompt injection.** Module 10 lesson 7. A user can put instructions in their message. If your bot can do anything beyond answering, this matters.

**Tone with an angry customer.** Generated empathy reads as insincere when someone is genuinely upset. Escalating is usually better than empathising.

**Being honest that it is a bot.** Module 8's disclosure lesson. Say so.

## What good looks like

A strong support project reports **both escalation numbers** -- correct escalations and false ones -- and has a defined, tested list of out-of-scope categories. A bot with no scope definition escalates on relevance alone, which misses the whole category of questions it could answer and should not.

lessons.title: Brief: AI research assistant
lessons.description: Highest hallucination risk in the module; every source from a real fetch.
lessons.content:
## The brief

A tool that helps research a topic: finds sources, summarises them, and reports what it could not establish.

### The smallest worthwhile version

1. **Take a research question** and break it into sub-questions
2. **Search** for each and collect sources
3. **Summarise** what was found, with citations
4. **State explicitly** what could not be established

Feature 4 is what makes this a research tool rather than a confident-answer generator.

### What makes this project

**This is the brief with the highest hallucination risk in the module**, because research is exactly where invention clusters: citations, statistics, attributed claims.

The design principle from module 6: **never ask the model for sources from memory.** Every source must come from an actual search with an actual URL, fetched and read. The model summarises what was fetched; it does not recall what exists.

If you cannot implement real search and fetching, change the design: have the user supply the sources, and build a tool that summarises and compares what they provide. That is a legitimate and well-scoped project, and it removes the risk entirely.

### Extensions

**Source quality assessment.** Flag what kind of source each is -- peer-reviewed, news, blog, marketing.

**Contradiction detection.** Where do these sources disagree?

**A reading list** ordered by what to read first.

**Follow-up questions** the research raised.

**Date awareness.** Flag sources older than a threshold.

### What to evaluate

**Citation validity.** Every URL: does it exist, and does it say what was attributed to it? **Check every single one.** This is the headline number and the whole point of the brief.

**Source quality.** Would you cite these yourself? Judge as a proportion.

**Coverage.** Did it find the sources you know exist on the topic?

**Honest gaps.** On a question with little good material available, did it say so or did it assemble something from weak sources?

### Watch out for

**Fabricated citations.** The defining risk. Every source must trace to a real URL that was actually fetched. If your tool produces a citation from the model's memory, that is a design flaw and it will score badly.

**Attribution drift.** A source says something qualified; the summary states it flatly. Check attributions against the original wording, not just that the source exists.

**Prompt injection from fetched pages.** Module 10 lesson 7. You are feeding external content into a model. A page can contain instructions.

**Agent scope.** If you build this as an agent -- module 11 -- set a step limit and a cost limit. A research agent in a loop is a research agent spending money.

## What good looks like

The strongest research projects **check every citation** and report the number that survived. A tool that produced twenty sources of which sixteen were real and said what was claimed is a good result, honestly reported. One that produced twenty and checked none scores poorly however good the summaries read.

lessons.title: Scoping and planning
lessons.description: Where most capstones are won or lost, before any code is written.
lessons.content:
## Learn

The planning lesson. Most capstone failures are scoping failures, and they are all preventable here.

### Write the smallest worthwhile version first

Before anything else, write down the smallest version that is still worth having.

Not what you hope to build. The minimum that would be useful to someone.

Then treat that as the project. Everything else is optional, and you only start it when the minimum works end to end.

### Why people get this wrong

**Features are easy to imagine and hard to finish.** Listing ten takes two minutes; building three properly takes the whole time.

**The last twenty per cent takes half the time.** Error handling, edge cases, deployment, evaluation. This is not pessimism; it is consistently true.

**Evaluation takes longer than you think.** Writing twenty test questions and marking twenty answers is an afternoon, and it is heavily weighted in the marking.

**Something will not work.** An API will change, extraction will fail, a library will not install. Budget for it.

### The plan

Write it down. Six parts:

**1. The one-paragraph statement** from lesson 1.

**2. The three features** of the minimum version. Exactly three, and no more.

**3. The evaluation plan**, written **now**, before building. What will you measure, on how many cases, and what counts as good? Writing this before you build stops you evaluating what the system happens to do well.

**4. The build order.** Smallest working thing first, then out. Something end to end early, even if each part is crude, beats one part perfected.

**5. The risks.** What might not work, and what you will do instead. "If PDF extraction is too poor, I will use plain text files and say so."

**6. What you will not build.** An explicit list. This is what you check against when tempted.

### Budgeting the time

A rough split that survives contact with reality:

- **20 per cent** setup and getting something end to end
- **30 per cent** the three core features
- **20 per cent** failure handling, refusal, edge cases
- **20 per cent** evaluation
- **10 per cent** writing it up and presenting

Notice that building is half. Everyone assumes it is ninety per cent, and the marking rewards the other half heavily.

### Build order

**End to end first, badly.** A version where every stage exists, even crudely. Then improve each.

The opposite -- perfecting extraction before writing any retrieval -- means discovering at the end that the pieces do not fit.

### Knowing when to stop

Stop adding features when:

- The three core features work
- Failure paths are handled
- The evaluation is done
- You have written it up

If time remains, **improve what exists** rather than adding. A fourth feature that half-works lowers your mark; a third feature that now refuses correctly raises it.

## Demonstrate

Write your plan now. Twenty minutes.

Use the six headings. Be specific enough that someone else could follow it.

Then do the hardest part: **take your feature list and cut it to three.** Write the removed ones under "what I will not build".

Almost everyone finds this uncomfortable and almost everyone who does it finishes.

## Practice

Take your plan and pressure-test it:

1. If you had **half** the time, which single feature would you keep?
2. What is the most likely thing to go wrong, and what is your alternative?
3. How long will the evaluation take? Multiply by 1.5.
4. What would "finished" look like? Write the sentence.

Question 1 is the useful one. That feature is your real project. Build it first, completely, before anything else.

## What to remember

- Write the smallest worthwhile version and treat that as the project
- Exactly three core features; write the rest under "will not build"
- Write the evaluation plan before building, not after
- Building is about half the work; evaluation and write-up are heavily marked
- End to end crudely first, then improve each stage
- With spare time, improve what exists rather than adding

lessons.title: Building it
lessons.description: The whole course's practices, collected for the week you are working.
lessons.content:
## Learn

The build. This lesson is the practices from the whole course, collected, for the week you are actually working.

### Start end to end

Day one: every stage exists and does something, however crudely. Input arrives, something happens, output appears.

You now know the pieces fit, and everything after is improvement rather than integration.

### One piece at a time

Module 9's discipline, and it matters most here. A contract, then the implementation, then run it, then the next.

Never generate a whole application. You cannot verify it.

### Version control from the start

```bash
git init
```

Before the first line. Commit when something works, with a message saying what.

And `.gitignore` before `.env` exists. Module 12's lesson, and the one that causes real incidents.

### Keep a build log

A file. Every session: what you did, what worked, what did not, what you changed.

Three reasons. It is most of your write-up already. It stops you repeating a failed approach. And it records the decisions you will otherwise forget by the time you present.

### Evaluate as you go

Do not leave it to the end.

Write your first five test cases after your first working feature. Run them. You will discover something you would otherwise have built on top of for a week.

### Handle failure early

Empty input, missing key, API failure, oversized input, no results. Handle them when you write each feature, not in a pass at the end.

A pass at the end always misses some, and they are what a user finds first.

### When you get stuck

**Reduce it.** Smallest code that still fails.

**Check the stages in order.** For RAG: extraction, chunking, embedding, retrieval, generation. The fault is usually earlier than you think.

**Print things.** The actual prompt sent, the actual chunks retrieved, the actual response. Most confusion dissolves at the moment you look at what is really being passed around.

**Ask for logging rather than a fix.** Module 9's most underused option.

**Step away after three failed attempts.** With a model, you are now in the guessing phase. Reset.

### Using AI to build it

Expected, and worth doing well.

**Keep the discipline.** Read everything, run everything, understand everything. Module 9.

**Log where it was wrong.** You need this for the write-up, and it is marked.

**Never accept code you cannot explain.** If asked about any line in your presentation, you should be able to answer.

### The week-before check

- Does it run from a clean checkout?
- Is `requirements.txt` complete?
- Is the key out of the code **and out of git history**?
- Does every failure path give a message, not a stack trace?
- Is the evaluation done, with numbers?
- Can someone else use it without you?

Check these a week early. Every one of them takes longer to fix than to check.

## Demonstrate

Here is a real build log entry, from the middle of a capstone. This is the format to copy.

```
2026-03-14, 90 min

Done:
- Chunking now prepends "[doc > section]" before embedding
- Re-ran the 15 test questions

Numbers:
- retrieval accuracy 9/15 -> 13/15 after the prefix change
- refusal rate still 0/5, the floor is not implemented yet

Broke:
- PDF extraction silently returned "" for the scanned appendix.
  Found it because chunk count was 40 lower than expected.
  Added a check: warn if a page yields under 20 characters.

Next:
1. Relevance floor (this is why refusal is 0)
2. Re-run all 20 cases
3. Handle the empty-input case in the CLI
```

Four things make this useful later. It has **numbers before and after** a change, so the write-up already has its evidence. It records **how a bug was noticed**, not just that it existed. It names **why** the next thing is next. And it is short enough that you will actually write it.

Compare that with what most people have at the end: a working project and no memory of what they tried.

## Practice

Set up properly, now, before writing any feature code:

1. `git init` and a first commit
2. `.gitignore` with `.env`
3. `.env.example`
4. A `BUILD_LOG.md` with today's date
5. A `tests/` folder or a test file, even empty
6. The one-paragraph project statement at the top of the README

Six things, fifteen minutes, and they prevent the six most common ways a capstone goes wrong.

## What to remember

- End to end on day one, however crude
- One piece at a time, with a contract, then run it
- Version control and `.gitignore` before the first line of code
- Keep a build log; it is most of your write-up and it stops repeated failures
- Write test cases after the first feature, not at the end
- Print the actual prompt and the actual retrieved chunks when confused

lessons.title: Testing and documenting
lessons.description: Test cases written first, including the ones it should fail.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Testing and documentation are where a project that works becomes a project that can be assessed -- and they are heavily weighted.

### The evaluation

The single most important part of your submission after the thing working.

**Write the test cases before you run them.** If you write them after seeing output, you will write ones it passes.

**Include cases it should fail.** Questions your documents cannot answer. Requests it should refuse. Inputs it should reject.

This is the number nobody measures and everybody should. A system that succeeds on everything you tried has not been tested; it has been demonstrated.

**Enough cases to mean something.** Twenty is a reasonable minimum. Five tells you nothing.

**Report per case, not just totals.** A table of twenty rows is evidence. "85 per cent" is a claim.

**Measure more than correctness.** Where it refused correctly. Where it cited correctly. Where it failed gracefully.

### What to measure, by project type

**Generation projects** -- study assistant, marketing: output quality against criteria you wrote, plus how often it invented something.

**RAG projects** -- PDF, support: retrieval accuracy, answer accuracy, citation accuracy, refusal rate.

**Agent projects** -- research: steps taken, actions that failed, whether it recovered, whether it reported what it could not do.

**All projects:** failure handling. Empty input, oversized input, no key, no network.

### Failure handling, tested

Write these down as test cases and actually run them:

- Every input empty
- One field empty
- Input far too long
- API key missing
- API key invalid
- Network unavailable
- A question with no answer available
- Input in an unexpected language
- Input containing something that looks like an instruction

The last is prompt injection from module 10, and it belongs in any project that reads content it did not write.

Each must produce a message, not a stack trace.

### The README

Someone else must be able to run it.

- What it does, in two sentences
- What it needs: Python version, dependencies, API access
- How to install
- How to configure -- naming environment variables, not values
- How to run
- A worked example with real input and real output
- **What it does badly**, plainly stated

The last section is marked and most people leave it out. A README that says "extraction from scanned PDFs does not work, and the tool does not currently detect this" is a better document than one that claims everything works.

### Documenting the code

Module 9's lesson: comment the **why**, not the what.

Docstrings on every function: what it takes, what it returns, what it raises.

And no `# TODO: why?` left in a submission. Answer them.

### Check it from clean

The step that catches what you cannot see:

```bash
git clone <your repo> /tmp/check
cd /tmp/check
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
# configure, then run
```

Missing dependencies, hard-coded paths, files you forgot to commit -- all surface here and nowhere else.

## Demonstrate

This is what a per-case results table looks like, and why totals alone are not enough.

A RAG project, 10 of its 20 cases shown:

- 1. "What is the notice period?" -- answerable -- correct, cited p.4 correctly
- 2. "How do I claim expenses?" -- answerable -- correct, cited p.11 correctly
- 3. "What is the dress code?" -- answerable -- **wrong**, cited p.2 which does not mention it
- 4. "Can I carry leave over?" -- answerable -- correct, cited p.7 correctly
- 5. "What is the parental leave policy?" -- answerable -- correct, **citation points at the wrong page**
- 6. "Who approves overtime?" -- answerable -- **refused**, should have answered
- 7. "What is the company's share price?" -- unanswerable -- correctly refused
- 8. "Who is the CEO?" -- unanswerable -- **answered anyway**, invented a name
- 9. "What is the office wifi password?" -- unanswerable -- correctly refused
- 10. "What are the pension contribution rates?" -- unanswerable -- correctly refused

The totals from this would read: answer accuracy 4/6, refusal rate 3/4. Respectable.

The per-case view shows three different problems the totals hide. Case 5 answered correctly with a **wrong citation**, which is worse than a wrong answer because it looks verified. Case 6 is a **false refusal** -- the information was there. Case 8 **invented a name**, which is the most serious failure in the set.

Three distinct faults, three different fixes, all invisible in "4/6 and 3/4". That is why the rubric asks for the table.

## Practice

Do the clean-checkout test now, before you think you are finished.

Then write down every problem it revealed. Most people find two or three, and the most common is a dependency installed weeks ago and never recorded.

Then write the "what it does badly" section of your README. Three specific things.

If you cannot think of three, you have not tested hard enough -- go back to the failure list above.
Every capstone needs the same small piece of code: something that runs your test cases and reports the numbers. Most people do it by hand in a spreadsheet, lose the results, and cannot show a before-and-after when they improve something.

### Exercise: a scoring harness

Write a function that takes your test cases and your system's answers and reports the numbers your report needs.

```python
def score(cases: list[dict], answers: list[dict]) -> dict:
    """Score a run against a test set.

    Each case is {'question': str, 'answerable': bool}.
    Each answer is {'correct': bool, 'refused': bool}, in the same order.

    Returns counts and rates for answerable and unanswerable cases
    separately, because a single overall accuracy hides the number
    that matters most.
    """
    # Your code here
    ...
```

Expected output for 3 answerable cases (2 correct) and 2 unanswerable (1 correctly refused):

```
{'answerable': 3, 'answered_correctly': 2, 'answer_accuracy': 0.667,
 'unanswerable': 2, 'correctly_refused': 1, 'refusal_rate': 0.5,
 'false_refusals': 0}
```

:::hint Getting started
Zip the cases and answers together and split into two groups on `case['answerable']`. For the answerable group, count `answer['correct']`; also count how many were refused when they should not have been -- that is `false_refusals`. For the unanswerable group, count `answer['refused']`. Guard both divisions against an empty group.
:::

:::solution
```python
def score(cases: list[dict], answers: list[dict]) -> dict:
    """Score a run against a test set."""
    if len(cases) != len(answers):
        raise ValueError(
            f"{len(cases)} cases but {len(answers)} answers -- they must line up"
        )

    answerable = [(c, a) for c, a in zip(cases, answers) if c["answerable"]]
    unanswerable = [(c, a) for c, a in zip(cases, answers) if not c["answerable"]]

    correct = sum(1 for _, a in answerable if a["correct"])
    refused_wrongly = sum(1 for _, a in answerable if a["refused"])
    refused_rightly = sum(1 for _, a in unanswerable if a["refused"])

    def rate(part: int, whole: int) -> float:
        return round(part / whole, 3) if whole else 0.0

    return {
        "answerable": len(answerable),
        "answered_correctly": correct,
        "answer_accuracy": rate(correct, len(answerable)),
        "unanswerable": len(unanswerable),
        "correctly_refused": refused_rightly,
        "refusal_rate": rate(refused_rightly, len(unanswerable)),
        "false_refusals": refused_wrongly,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    cases = [
        {"question": "q1", "answerable": True},
        {"question": "q2", "answerable": True},
        {"question": "q3", "answerable": True},
        {"question": "q4", "answerable": False},
        {"question": "q5", "answerable": False},
    ]
    answers = [
        {"correct": True, "refused": False},
        {"correct": True, "refused": False},
        {"correct": False, "refused": False},
        {"correct": False, "refused": True},
        {"correct": False, "refused": False},
    ]
    print(score(cases, answers))
```

Output:

```
{'answerable': 3, 'answered_correctly': 2, 'answer_accuracy': 0.667, 'unanswerable': 2, 'correctly_refused': 1, 'refusal_rate': 0.5, 'false_refusals': 0}
```

Three deliberate choices. The length check fails immediately rather than silently scoring against misaligned data, which `zip` would otherwise do by truncating. `false_refusals` is tracked separately because a system that refuses everything scores a perfect refusal rate and is useless -- you need both directions to see where yours sits. And `rate` returns 0.0 rather than raising on an empty group, so a test set with no unanswerable cases still produces a report -- one that visibly shows `unanswerable: 0`, which is exactly the omission the rubric penalises.
:::

### Debugging exercise

This is meant to report which cases got worse after a change. It has **two** bugs.

```python
def regressions(before: list[dict], after: list[dict]) -> list[int]:
    worse = []
    for i in range(len(before)):
        if before[i]["correct"] and not after[i]["correct"]:
            worse.append(i)
    return worse
```

:::hint What to look at
Run it where `after` is shorter than `before` -- you added a test case and re-ran only some of them. Then think about what a reader of your report needs from the index this returns.
:::

:::solution
**Bug one: it indexes `after` using `before`'s length.** If the two runs have different numbers of cases -- which happens the moment you add a test case -- this raises `IndexError`, or worse, compares case 7 of one run with case 7 of a differently-ordered other run.

**Bug two: it returns bare indices.** An index is useless in a report. You need to know *which question* regressed, and a list of integers sends you back to cross-reference by hand.

```python
def regressions(before: list[dict], after: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
    """Cases that were correct before a change and are not after."""
    if len(before) != len(after):
        raise ValueError(
            f"{len(before)} cases before but {len(after)} after -- "
            "re-run the full test set so the comparison is valid"
        )

    return [
        {"index": index, "question": old.get("question", "(unknown)")}
        for index, (old, new) in enumerate(zip(before, after))
        if old["correct"] and not new["correct"]
    ]
```

Bug one is the instructive one, and it is a version of a mistake from module 13: two parallel lists that must stay aligned, where nothing checks that they do. When they drift, the function still returns a plausible list of regressions, all of them wrong.

Use this after every change you make in section 7 of your report. A change that fixes three cases and breaks two is a change worth knowing about, and it is invisible in a single overall percentage.
:::

## What to remember

- Write test cases before running them, and include cases it should fail
- Twenty cases minimum, reported per case, not as a percentage
- Measure refusal and citation accuracy, not just correctness
- Test every failure path: empty, oversized, no key, no network, injection
- A README section saying what it does badly is marked, and most people omit it
- Clone to a clean directory and run it; it always finds something

lessons.title: Presenting your work
lessons.description: Show what it does, that it works, and that you know its limits.
lessons.content:
## Learn

You present the capstone. This is Level 3 of the certification, and the presentation is part of it.

### What a presentation is for

Not to prove you worked hard. To show someone **what it does, that it works, and that you understand its limits**.

The third is what separates a strong presentation from a demo, and it is the part people cut when short of time. Do not.

### The structure

**Ten minutes**, roughly:

**1. The problem, 1 minute.** What need, for whom. Concrete and specific.

**2. What it does, 1 minute.** In plain language. No architecture yet.

**3. Demonstration, 3 minutes.** Show it working, live if you can.

**4. How it works, 2 minutes.** The pipeline, at the level of boxes and arrows. Not a code walkthrough.

**5. Evaluation, 2 minutes.** Your numbers. What you measured, on how many cases, what the results were.

**6. Limits and what is next, 1 minute.** What it does badly, honestly.

Section 5 is where most presentations are weakest and where the marks are.

### The demonstration

**Rehearse it.** At least twice, fully, with the real application.

**Have a recording as backup.** Live demonstrations fail. A thirty-second screen recording means a failure costs you nothing.

**Use real input**, prepared in advance. Do not type a long prompt live.

**Show a failure deliberately.** Ask it something your documents cannot answer, and show it refusing. This is the most impressive thing in most capstone demonstrations, because almost nobody does it and it proves the system has judgement.

**Do not show every feature.** Two, properly, beats five rushed.

### Presenting the evaluation

Specific numbers, not adjectives.

Weak: *"It works well and gives accurate answers."*

Strong: *"I tested 20 questions. 15 it should answer, 5 it should not. It answered 13 of 15 correctly with correct citations. It correctly refused 4 of the 5. The one it should have refused was about a topic my documents mention in passing, which I think is a borderline case."*

The second sentence is worth far more, and the last clause -- the honest note about the borderline case -- is worth more still.

### The questions

Expect these. Prepare an answer for each:

- **"What does it do badly?"** Have three ready.
- **"What would you do differently?"** Not "nothing".
- **"How do you know it works?"** Your numbers.
- **"What happens if [edge case]?"** Know your failure paths.
- **"Why this approach rather than X?"** Know one alternative you rejected and why.
- **"Explain this line of code."** You must be able to.

That last one is why module 9 said not to keep code you cannot explain.

### Common mistakes

**Too much architecture.** Nobody needs your file structure.

**A live demo with no backup.**

**Hiding the limits.** Naming them makes you more credible, not less. An audience that finds a limit you did not mention trusts everything else less.

**Claims without numbers.**

**Overrunning.** Rehearse with a timer.

## Demonstrate

The same evaluation, presented two ways. Read both aloud.

**Weak:**

> I tested it quite thoroughly and it works well. The answers are accurate and it usually gets the citations right. There are a few edge cases where it struggles but overall I am happy with the results.

**Strong:**

> I tested 20 questions: 15 my documents answer and 5 they do not. It answered 13 of the 15 correctly. Citations were right on 12 -- one answer was correct but cited the wrong page, which I think is the worse failure because it looks verified. It correctly refused 4 of the 5 it should not answer. The one it answered was about a topic my documents mention in passing, so I think that is a borderline case rather than a clean failure.

The second takes twenty seconds longer and does four things the first cannot. It gives a **denominator**. It separates **answering** from **citing**. It reports the **refusal** number, which almost nobody measures. And it offers a **judgement** about which failure matters more, which is what shows you understand your own system rather than just having run it.

Write your version of the second one out in full and read it aloud before you present. It is the hardest thirty seconds of the talk to improvise.

## Practice

Write your presentation as bullet points under the six headings, then rehearse it twice with a timer.

Then do the part that matters: **give it to one person** and ask them, afterwards, two questions:

1. What does it do?
2. What is it not good at?

If they cannot answer both, the presentation needs work, and it is almost always section 6 that was rushed.

Record their answers. That is your evidence that the presentation works, exactly as the lab in module 7 used a person to test a poster.

## What to remember

- Show what it does, that it works, and that you know its limits
- Rehearse the demonstration twice and record a backup
- Demonstrate a deliberate refusal; almost nobody does and it proves judgement
- Evaluation with specific numbers beats any adjective
- Prepare answers to the six predictable questions
- Naming your limits makes you more credible, not less

lessons.title: Practice questions and answer key
lessons.description: Ten questions on scoping, evaluating and presenting a capstone.
lessons.content:
Ten questions on the capstone module.

:::quiz
Q. What is the most common cause of capstone failure?
- Technical difficulty
+ Choosing a project too large to finish
- Poor choice of model
- Insufficient AI assistance
= Almost everyone chooses something too big. Write the smallest worthwhile version down and treat that as the project; a small thing that works and is measured beats a large thing that half-works, by a wide margin.

Q. When should you write your evaluation plan?
- After the first feature works
+ Before you build anything
- After building, so you know what to measure
- At the same time as the write-up
= Criteria written after seeing output are unconsciously shaped to what the output happened to do. This is module 4's lesson applied to a whole project.

Q. Roughly what share of capstone time should go to building the features?
- About ninety per cent
- About seventy per cent
+ About thirty per cent
- About ten per cent
= Setup and end-to-end is about twenty per cent, features thirty, failure handling twenty, evaluation twenty, write-up ten. Everyone assumes building is nearly all of it, and the marking rewards the other half heavily.

Q. What must a test set include to be worth anything?
- At least fifty cases
+ Cases the system should fail or refuse, not only ones it should pass
- Cases drawn from the training data
- An equal number of easy and hard cases
= A system that succeeds on everything you tried has been demonstrated, not tested. The refusal rate is the number nobody measures and everybody should.

Q. In the resume assistant brief, what is the headline number?
- How many bullets it rewrote
+ How often it invented a skill or achievement not in the CV
- How many interview questions it generated
- Keyword coverage against the job description
= Without an explicit no-invention rule these tools routinely add achievements, which is useless and genuinely serious to send to an employer. The "gaps" section turns that temptation into the most useful output.

Q. In a PDF question-answering project, where should most of the time go?
- Choosing the embedding model
+ PDF text extraction
- Prompt engineering
- The user interface
= Two columns extract as interleaved nonsense, headers repeat into every chunk, tables become word salad, and scanned pages contain no text at all. Extraction problems are invisible later: the answers are simply wrong with no indication why.

Q. Why should a research assistant never ask the model for sources from memory?
- It is slower than searching
+ Citations are exactly where invention clusters; every source must come from a real fetch
- Models refuse to provide citations
- Search results are more recent
= If you cannot implement real search and fetching, change the design so the user supplies the sources. That is a legitimate, well-scoped project and it removes the risk entirely.

Q. What is the most impressive thing to include in a capstone demonstration?
- Showing every feature
- A detailed architecture diagram
+ Deliberately showing it refuse something it cannot answer
- The size of the codebase
= Almost nobody does this, and it proves the system has judgement rather than just producing output. It is also the evidence that your refusal path actually works.

Q. How should you present your evaluation?
- As an overall percentage
+ Specific numbers, per case, including the cases it got wrong
- As a summary of what worked well
- With a chart rather than numbers
= "I tested 20 questions, 15 answerable and 5 not; it answered 13 correctly and refused 4 of the 5" is worth far more than "it works well". The honest note about the borderline case is worth more still.

Q. What should you do with spare time at the end of a capstone?
- Add a fourth feature
+ Improve what already exists, especially failure handling and evaluation
- Refactor the code
- Improve the user interface styling
= A fourth feature that half-works lowers your mark. A third feature that now refuses correctly, or an evaluation extended from ten cases to twenty, raises it.
:::

## How to read your score

Seven or more and you are ready to build. If you missed questions about scoping or evaluation, reread lessons 8 and 10 before you start -- those are the two that decide most capstone outcomes.

lessons.title: Hands-on lab: the build sprint
lessons.description: Ninety minutes from nothing to end-to-end working.
lessons.content:
Ninety minutes. A focused build sprint to get your capstone from nothing to end-to-end working.

The goal is **not** a finished project. It is a version where every stage exists and does something, so you know the pieces fit.

## Before you start

You need your plan from lesson 8: the one-paragraph statement, the three features, the evaluation plan, and the list of what you will not build.

If you do not have it, write it now. Twenty minutes spent here saves hours.

## Minutes 0-15: Setup

```bash
mkdir capstone && cd capstone
git init
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
```

Create, in this order:

1. `.gitignore` with `.env`, `__pycache__/`, `.venv/`
2. `.env.example` with the variable names, no values
3. `.env` with your real values
4. `README.md` with your one-paragraph statement
5. `BUILD_LOG.md` with today's date

Commit. `git status` must not show `.env`.

## Minutes 15-40: The thinnest end-to-end path

One path through your system, working, however crude.

Not the best version. The **simplest** one:

- **RAG project:** one document, split naively by paragraph, embedded, one question answered
- **Generation project:** one prompt, one input, one output printed
- **Agent project:** one tool, one step, one result

Hard-code things. Skip error handling. Print instead of building an interface.

**You must reach a working end-to-end path in these 25 minutes.** If you cannot, your project is too large -- cut it now, not in week three.

Commit it.

## Minutes 40-55: Five test cases

Before improving anything.

Write five cases: three it should handle, two it should refuse or reject.

Run them. Record the results in your build log.

:::hint It fails the two it should refuse
Expected, and it is the most useful thing you will learn in this sprint. You have not built a refusal path yet. Note exactly what it did instead -- almost always it produced a confident answer from irrelevant material -- and add the refusal path in the next block. Discovering this now rather than in week three is the point of writing the test cases early.
:::

## Minutes 55-75: Failure paths

Now make it fail properly. Handle, at minimum:

- Empty input
- Missing API key, with a clear message
- API call failure
- Input too long
- Nothing relevant found, if you retrieve

Each must produce a message, not a stack trace.

Re-run your five test cases. The two that should be refused should now be refused.

Commit.

## Minutes 75-85: The second feature

Only now. Add your second core feature, reusing what exists.

If this takes longer than ten minutes, that is information about your scope.

## Minutes 85-90: Log and plan

In your build log, write:

1. What works end to end now
2. What broke and how you fixed it
3. The single most uncertain thing remaining
4. The next three things, in order

## Write it up

1. Your end-to-end path, and how long it took to reach
2. Your five test cases and their results, before and after the failure-handling block
3. What surprised you
4. Your honest assessment of whether the scope is right

## What good looks like

A successful sprint **reaches end to end**, even crudely. That is the whole measure.

The most valuable outcome is discovering your scope is too large, at minute forty rather than in week three. If that is what you found, say so and say what you are cutting. That is a successful sprint, not a failed one.

lessons.title: Assignment: capstone submission and presentation
lessons.description: The Level 3 certification, marked against a published rubric.
lessons.content:
## The task

Build, evaluate, document and present a working generative AI application.

This is the Level 3 certification. It assesses everything in the course.

## What to submit

Four things:

1. **The code**, in a repository
2. **The application**, running -- deployed, or runnable from a clean checkout
3. **A report**, 1500 to 2000 words
4. **A presentation**, 10 minutes

## 1. The application

**Three core features minimum**, working.

**Every failure path handled.** No stack trace reachable by a user.

**Refuses when it should.** Whatever that means for your project: outside its documents, outside its scope, or input it should reject.

**Runs from a clean checkout** with a README someone else could follow.

## 2. The repository

- All source
- `requirements.txt` that works from clean
- `.env.example` present; `.env` absent
- README: what it does, install, configure, run, a worked example, **and what it does badly**
- Your build log
- Your test cases and results

**No key anywhere, including git history.** Check with `git log -p | grep -i "sk-\|api_key\|secret"`.

## 3. The report

**1. The project.** What, for whom, why. Your one-paragraph statement, expanded.

**2. What it does.** The three features, and what you deliberately did not build.

**3. How it works.** The pipeline, the key decisions and what you rejected. Include your prompts in full.

**4. The evaluation.** The heaviest-marked section.

- Your test set: **minimum 20 cases**, including **at least 5 it should refuse or reject**
- Your criteria, written before you ran anything
- **Per-case results**, as a table
- The measurements appropriate to your project: accuracy, citation accuracy, refusal rate, invention rate, recovery rate
- What the numbers actually say

**5. Failure analysis.** **Three** things it gets wrong. For each: what happens, why, which part of the system is responsible, what would fix it.

"The model got it wrong" is not a diagnosis. Name the stage.

**6. Where AI helped and where it did not.** Honest. Including at least two places an assistant gave you something wrong, how you noticed, and what you did.

**7. Limits.** What it should not be used for. Who should not rely on it. What would need to be true before it could be.

**8. What you learned.** Genuinely. Including what you would do differently.

## 4. The presentation

Ten minutes, the structure from lesson 11.

Must include a **live or recorded demonstration**, and must include **showing it refuse something**.

Be ready for: what does it do badly, how do you know it works, explain this line of code.

## Rubric

Marked out of 100.

**The application, 25 marks.** Full marks for three features working, every failure path handled, correct refusal, and someone else able to run it. Marks lost per broken feature and heavily for any reachable stack trace.

**Evaluation, 30 marks.** Full marks for 20+ cases including 5+ it should refuse, criteria written in advance, per-case results shown, and the measurements appropriate to the project type. **An evaluation without cases it should fail cannot score above half.** This is the heaviest section in the course.

**Failure analysis, 15 marks.** Full marks for three failures each traced to a specific part of the system with evidence and a proposed fix. Marks lost for generic failures and for blaming the model without naming a stage.

**Repository and documentation, 10 marks.** Full marks for a clean checkout that runs, complete requirements, `.env.example`, a README including what it does badly, and no key in history. **A key found in the repository or history scores zero for this section**, and revoke it immediately.

**Honest account of AI assistance, 10 marks.** Full marks for a genuine account including at least two things an assistant got wrong and how you caught them. A submission claiming no errors is not credible.

**Presentation, 10 marks.** Full marks for a clear ten minutes covering problem, demonstration including a refusal, evaluation with numbers, and limits -- plus answering questions well.

## What will cost you marks

**A test set with nothing it should fail.** The most common and most expensive omission.

**Percentages without per-case results.**

**"The model got it wrong."** Name the stage.

**Claiming no AI errors.** Not credible across a whole project.

**A stack trace a user can reach.** Test every field empty, enormous, and with the network off.

**A key in history.** Check before submitting.

**Code you cannot explain.** You will be asked.

## The bar

A project that scores well is **small, working, measured and honestly described**.

It is not the most ambitious project. Every year the highest marks go to modest projects that work reliably, were properly evaluated, and whose author can say exactly what they do badly -- and the lowest go to ambitious ones that half-work and were never measured.

:::hint I have run out of time and my third feature does not work
Cut it. A submission with two features that work, handle failure and are properly evaluated scores substantially higher than three where one is broken. Remove it from the code, say in the report that you scoped it out and why, and spend the remaining time on the evaluation -- which is worth thirty marks against the five or so you would gain from a third feature. Scoping down under time pressure and saying so is a professional judgement, and it is marked as one.
:::
